points.description: Mentions holding the mass of one element fixed (constant) when comparing the compounds, e.g. 'a fixed mass of one element' or 'the same amount of one element'. Accept equivalent wording.
Refers to the mass data used in the Law of Multiple Proportions, i.e. measured masses of the elements in the compounds are compared. Accept 'uses mass data', 'compares masses', or equivalent.
States that the elements combine to form compounds, especially more than one compound. Accept 'form compounds', 'make different compounds', or equivalent.

States that the masses combining with the fixed mass are in an integer/whole-number ratio, e.g. 1:2 or 2:3. Accept 'simple whole-number ratio' or 'ratio of small whole numbers'; do not accept a mere 'ratio' without whole-number/integer.
Explains that the whole-number ratio implies matter is made of discrete/indivisible particles, or that matter cannot be continuous/divisible indefinitely.

levels.says: Says whole-number ratios suggest particles or units, but does not state that they are indivisible/discrete.

points.description: Concludes that the indivisible unit or particle of mass is the atom. Accept wording that identifies atoms as the indivisible units of mass.

levels.says: Mentions atoms as the basic particles or units but does not explicitly identify them as the indivisible unit of mass.

rubric.notes: Full marks require all six ideas: fixed mass of one element, mass data, compound formation, whole-number ratio, whole numbers implying indivisible/discrete particles, and the indivisible unit of mass being the atom. P5 and P6 can earn half credit when the idea is present but vague or incomplete. No marks are earned for saying only that atoms are small or that matter is made of atoms without linking this to the whole-number mass ratios.
